## Why Go Beyond Plain SQL?

SQL is **declarative** — great for describing *what* you want, clumsy for *how* to compute it step by step. Sometimes you need loops, conditionals, and reusable logic. SQL:1999 added **functions, procedures, and control-flow constructs** to bridge that gap, turning SQL into something closer to a general-purpose language.

```{=html}
<div class="flow"><div class="box"><b>Functions</b><span>return a value or a table</span></div><div class="box"><b>Procedures</b><span>return results through out parameters</span></div><div class="box"><b>Constructs</b><span>loops, if, case, exceptions</span></div><div class="box"><b>Triggers</b><span>run automatically on a change</span></div></div>
```

::: {.callout-note title="Note"}
The lecture syntax below is the **SQL standard**. PostgreSQL (used by the course datasets) writes the same ideas in its procedural language **PL/pgSQL**, so each standard example is followed by a version you can run.
:::

---

## SQL Functions

A **function** returns a single value, and can be written in SQL itself — or in an external language (useful for specialized types like images or geometry, e.g. "do these two polygons overlap?").

```sql
create function dept_count(dept_name varchar(20))
returns integer
begin
    declare d_count integer;
    select count(*) into d_count
    from instructor
    where instructor.dept_name = dept_name;
    return d_count;
end
```

The same function in PostgreSQL, on the university dataset:

```{.sql db="university"}
create or replace function dept_count(d_name varchar(20))
returns integer as $$
declare
    d_count integer;
begin
    select count(*) into d_count
    from instructor
    where instructor.dept_name = d_name;
    return d_count;
end;
$$ language plpgsql;
```

Use it just like any expression:

```{.sql db="university"}
select dept_name, budget
from department
where dept_count(dept_name) > 4;
```

| Keyword | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `begin ... end` | A **compound statement** — holds multiple SQL statements together |
| `returns` | Declares the *type* of the result (e.g., `integer`) |
| `return` | Specifies the *actual value* sent back when the function finishes |

::: {.callout-note title="Key idea"}
Think of SQL functions as **parameterized views** — a view that generalizes by accepting arguments.
:::

### Table Functions

Added in SQL:2003 — instead of returning one value, a table function returns an **entire relation**.

```sql
create function instructor_of(dept_name varchar(20))
returns table (
    id varchar(5),
    name varchar(20),
    dept_name varchar(20),
    salary numeric(8,2)
)
return table
    (select id, name, dept_name, salary
     from instructor
     where instructor.dept_name = instructor_of.dept_name);

select * from table(instructor_of('Biology'));
```

In PostgreSQL, the function is called directly in `from`:

```{.sql db="university"}
create or replace function instructor_of(d_name varchar(20))
returns table (id varchar(5), name varchar(20),
               dept_name varchar(20), salary numeric(8,2)) as $$
    select i.id, i.name, i.dept_name, i.salary
    from instructor as i
    where i.dept_name = d_name;
$$ language sql;

select * from instructor_of('Biology');
```

### Procedures

Where a function returns a value via `return`, a **procedure** passes results back through `out` parameters.

```sql
create procedure dept_count_proc(
    in dept_name varchar(20),
    out d_count integer)
begin
    select count(*) into d_count
    from instructor
    where instructor.dept_name = dept_count_proc.dept_name;
end

declare d_count integer;
call dept_count_proc('Physics', d_count);
```

```{.sql db="university"}
create or replace procedure dept_count_proc(
    in d_name varchar(20),
    out d_count integer) as $$
begin
    select count(*) into d_count
    from instructor
    where instructor.dept_name = d_name;
end;
$$ language plpgsql;

call dept_count_proc('Physics', null);
```

::: {.callout-note title="Note"}
SQL:1999 allows **overloading** — multiple functions/procedures can share a name as long as their parameter count or types differ.
:::

## Procedural Language Constructs

::: {.callout-note title="Note"}
Most databases implement their own dialect of these — syntax varies across systems.
:::

### Loops

```sql
-- while: check condition before each iteration
while boolean_expression do
    sequence_of_statements;
end while;

-- repeat: check condition after each iteration (always runs once)
repeat
    sequence_of_statements;
until boolean_expression
end repeat;

-- for: iterate directly over query results
declare total integer default 0;
for r as
    select budget from department
do
    set total = total + r.budget;
end for;
```

The `for` loop above, run in PostgreSQL as a function that returns the total:

```{.sql db="university"}
create or replace function total_budget() returns numeric as $$
declare
    total numeric := 0;
    r record;
begin
    for r in select budget from department loop
        total := total + r.budget;
    end loop;
    return total;
end;
$$ language plpgsql;

select total_budget();
```

```{=html}
<div class="flow steps"><div class="step"><div class="box"><b>fetch next row</b></div><span>into r</span></div><div class="arrow">→</div><div class="step"><div class="box"><b>add</b></div><span>total := total + r.budget</span></div><div class="arrow">→</div><div class="step"><div class="box"><b>repeat</b></div><span>until no rows remain</span></div></div>
```

### Conditionals

```sql
-- if / elseif / else
if boolean_expression then
    sequence_of_statements;
elseif boolean_expression then
    sequence_of_statements;
else
    sequence_of_statements;
end if;
```

```sql
-- simple case: match a variable against fixed values
case dept_name
    when 'Biology' then ...
    when 'Physics' then ...
    else ...
end case;

-- searched case: match arbitrary expressions
case
    when salary > 100000 then ...
    when salary > 50000 then ...
    else ...
end case;
```

A searched `case` on the university dataset (inside a query, `case` ends with `end`):

```{.sql db="university"}
select name, salary,
       case
           when salary > 100000 then 'high'
           when salary > 50000 then 'medium'
           else 'low'
       end as band
from instructor;
```

### Exception Handling

```sql
declare out_of_classroom_seats condition;
declare exit handler for out_of_classroom_seats
begin
    ...
    signal out_of_classroom_seats;
    ...
end
```

The `exit` handler terminates the enclosing `begin...end` block when the condition fires. Other handler behaviors are also possible (e.g., continue instead of exit).

In PostgreSQL, an `exception` section handles the error (and `raise exception` signals your own):

```{.sql db="university"}
create or replace function add_instructor(i_id varchar(5), i_name varchar(20),
                                          d_name varchar(20), sal numeric)
returns text as $$
begin
    insert into instructor values (i_id, i_name, d_name, sal);
    return 'added ' || i_name;
exception
    when unique_violation then
        return 'id ' || i_id || ' already exists';
end;
$$ language plpgsql;

select add_instructor('63395', 'Copy', 'Biology', 50000);   -- id already exists
```

## Triggers

A **trigger** is code that fires automatically in response to an `insert`, `update`, or `delete` on a table — no one has to remember to call it.

Defining a trigger means specifying three things:

1. **Event** — insert / update / delete
2. **Timing** — `BEFORE` or `AFTER` the event
3. **Action** — what to actually do

```{=html}
<div class="flow steps"><div class="step"><div class="box"><b>Event</b></div><span>insert / update / delete</span></div><div class="arrow">→</div><div class="step"><div class="box"><b>BEFORE trigger</b></div><span>validate or modify values first</span></div><div class="arrow">→</div><div class="step"><div class="box"><b>Database operation</b></div><span>executes</span></div><div class="arrow">→</div><div class="step"><div class="box"><b>AFTER trigger</b></div><span>update other tables, audit, alert</span></div></div>
```

### BEFORE vs. AFTER

| Timing | Typical use |
|---|---|
| **BEFORE** | Clean up or validate incoming values before they're written (e.g., normalize blanks to `null`); raise errors before a delete proceeds |
| **AFTER** | Update *other* tables to stay in sync, maintain audit trails, enforce cross-table integrity, trigger alerts/notifications |

### Row-Level vs. Statement-Level

| Type | Behavior |
|---|---|
| **Row-level** | Fires once **per affected row**. A 10% raise across 100 instructors fires the trigger 100 times. |
| **Statement-level** | Fires **once per statement**, regardless of how many rows were touched — uses `referencing old table` / `referencing new table` to access all affected rows at once via transition tables. More efficient for bulk updates. |

### Example: BEFORE trigger (data cleanup)

Convert blank grades to `null` before they're written:

```sql
create trigger setnull_trigger before update of grade on takes
referencing new row as nrow
for each row
when (nrow.grade = ' ')
begin atomic
    set nrow.grade = null;
end;
```

In PostgreSQL a trigger calls a **trigger function**:

```{.sql db="university"}
create or replace function setnull_grade() returns trigger as $$
begin
    if new.grade = ' ' then
        new.grade := null;
    end if;
    return new;
end;
$$ language plpgsql;

drop trigger if exists setnull_trigger on takes;
create trigger setnull_trigger
before update of grade on takes
for each row
execute function setnull_grade();
```

```{.sql db="university"}
begin;
update takes set grade = ' ' where id = '1000' and course_id = '642';
select id, course_id, grade from takes where id = '1000' and course_id = '642';
rollback;
```

### Example: AFTER trigger (cross-table maintenance)

Update a student's earned credits whenever a failing/blank grade turns into a pass:

```sql
create trigger credits_earned after update of grade on takes
referencing new row as nrow
referencing old row as orow
for each row
when nrow.grade <> 'F' and nrow.grade is not null
     and (orow.grade = 'F' or orow.grade is null)
begin atomic
    update student
    set tot_cred = tot_cred +
        (select credits from course where course.course_id = nrow.course_id)
    where student.id = nrow.id;
end;
```

```{.sql db="university"}
create or replace function credits_earned() returns trigger as $$
begin
    update student
    set tot_cred = tot_cred +
        (select credits from course where course.course_id = new.course_id)
    where student.id = new.id;
    return new;
end;
$$ language plpgsql;

drop trigger if exists credits_earned on takes;
create trigger credits_earned
after update of grade on takes
for each row
when (new.grade <> 'F' and new.grade is not null
      and (old.grade = 'F' or old.grade is null))
execute function credits_earned();
```

```{.sql db="university"}
begin;
select tot_cred from student where id = '1000';
update takes set grade = 'F' where id = '1000' and course_id = '642';
update takes set grade = 'B' where id = '1000' and course_id = '642';   -- F becomes a pass
select tot_cred from student where id = '1000';                         -- 3 credits added
rollback;
```

```{=html}
<div class="table-wrap"><table class="jt res"><tr><th>Update</th><th>old → new grade</th><th>Trigger fires?</th></tr><tr><td>set grade = 'F'</td><td>C- → F</td><td>no: new grade is F</td></tr><tr><td>set grade = 'B'</td><td>F → B</td><td>yes: tot_cred + 3</td></tr></table></div>
```

- `referencing old row as` — access pre-update values (deletes & updates)
- `referencing new row as` — access post-update values (inserts & updates)
- Triggers can be scoped to specific columns: `after update of grade on takes`

---

## Using Triggers Wisely

### Good Uses

- Logging changes to a history/audit table
- Recording metadata an application can't see (who ran it, when, from where)
- Simple, self-contained validation
- Keeping denormalized or derived values in sync

### When to Avoid Triggers

| Risk | Why it hurts |
|---|---|
| Too many triggers | Hard to trace *why* something changed |
| Complex trigger logic | Business logic buried where developers won't look |
| Cross-server triggers | Network calls hidden inside what looks like a simple `update` |
| Triggers calling triggers | Cascading side effects, hard to predict |
| Recursive triggers enabled | Can spiral — off by default for a reason |
| Views/procedures/functions nested inside triggers | Performance black box |
| Iteration inside triggers | Row-by-row processing at scale = slow |

**Rule of thumb:** triggers are best for short, simple, self-contained operations — not as a substitute for your application's business logic.
